title: Crystal Palace, the National Sports Centre and why a return home was an impossible dream
text:
Flaking blue paintwork on the concrete surround of Crystal Palace National Sports Centre Matt Woosnam/The Athletic

The scene is desolate. The Crystal Palace National Sports Centre is in a state of disrepair; unloved, underappreciated. The park that surrounds it may be full of life, thriving as a hub for its corner of south-east London, but decades of little to no use have left the arena run-down and ramshackle.

Advertisement

The stands are weathered, the blue exterior paintwork blistered and peeling to leave the concrete beneath exposed. The seats in the Jubilee Stand, built in 1977 and the smaller of the two covered blocks, are sun-faded.

Fabric attached to the roof has torn and now flaps in the breeze, while nature is reclaiming the surrounds. Weeds spring up through cracks in the tarmac. The steps that lead through blocks 12 to 14 are strewn with fallen branches. Moss has taken hold.

This is the stadium time forgot.

Except, there are some still finding a use for it.

The athletics track remains intact, and a handful of runners are training there when The Athletic visits. They are actually following in the footsteps of giants — Sebastian Coe, Linford Christie and others from the cream of British athletics once graced this scene — though now their voices merely echo eerily around the empty bowl.

None of this sounds like much of an opportunity.

Yet, following a May 2023 pledge from mayor of London Sadiq Khan, a planning application was submitted in March this year for the regeneration of this stadium, including the outside sports pitches and the Grade II-listed indoor centre, with its 50m Olympic-sized swimming pool.

Millions of pounds will be invested to turn the site into something of which the UK’s capital can once again be proud, just as it was after opening in 1964 when it stood as one of the nation’s premier athletic venues.

The sports centre was built just beside the terrace of the original Crystal Palace. The huge structure, flanked by imposing water towers, housed the spoils of the British Empire until it burned down in 1936 but, while it stood, top-level cricket and football, including the FA Cup final, were played here.

It was also the first home of the modern-day Crystal Palace Football Club, formed in 1905 but inspired by an amateur team who first played here back in 1861.

Advertisement

Yet, while plans have often been mooted to move the club back to their original home, it is unlikely to be football which rescues this site from its dilapidated state. That ship has long since sailed. Palace, instead, will look to redevelop Selhurst Park, their home since 1924, even if some will always cast covetous glances up the hill.

Crystal Palace FC and the National Sports Centre (NSC) will forever be a story of missed opportunities.

This spot’s association with elite sport dates back far further than the 1960s.

The original Crystal Palace, a vast iron and glass building first erected by Sir Joseph Paxton in central London’s Hyde Park for the Great Exhibition in 1851 before its relocation to Sydenham Hill, south London, stood just above where the sports centre now crumbles. The terracing is currently being restored.

This is one of London’s highest vantage points, at 367ft (112m) above sea level. The night the palace burned down 90 years ago, the glow could be seen in northern France.

But while it stood, it was effectively the nation’s greatest pleasure park.

The building hosted orchestral concerts and a circus, exhibitions, festivals and fetes. There were cat shows, dog shows, even pigeon shows. Visitors, including world leaders, came to marvel at artefacts from around the British Empire.

Landscaped gardens housed the celebrated dinosaur sculptures, first unveiled in 1854 and, although inaccurate by modern scientific standards, still a draw to this day (albeit they, too, are currently being restored).

It was also a home for all manner of sports: from cricket, baseball, rugby union and league, basketball and wrestling, to tennis and motor racing.

Football was the main draw, though. The FA Cup final was played in the grounds of the Palace each year from 1895 to 1914, with the 1901 match drawing a crowd of 110,000.

Advertisement

Its popularity and status made it a target as the Suffragettes ramped up their campaign to win the right for women to vote by targeting sporting events, and there was a plot in April 1913 to blow up the stadium grandstands on that year’s FA Cup final day. That scheme was foiled.

By 1937, with the main build having burned down, a motor-racing circuit was established in the park — and remained in use for the following 35 years — while the NSC opened in 1964, one of five such centres across the country run on behalf of Sport England. It occupied the same land on which the original stadium was built.

Coe, the two-time Olympic gold medalist middle-distance runner and current president of World Athletics, and sprinter Christie were once regulars on its track. So, too, was another multiple gold-medalist middle-distance star, Kelly Holmes. Decorated decathlete, Daley Thompson, pulled up injured at the stadium when attempting to qualify for the 1992 Olympic Games. It was to be his final appearance before retirement.

Yet its significance waned, particularly when resources were poured instead into developing the arena in Stratford, east London, which went on to host the 2012 Olympics.

In May 1982, Pope John Paul II had arrived by helicopter to address around 24,000 members of the Polish community in the stadium on Pentecost Sunday as part of the papacy’s first visit to the UK.

These days, while the park remains popular, the biggest crowds attracted to the area are generally for music concerts and festivals, with Crystal Palace having attracted artists including Bob Marley, Pink Floyd, the Rolling Stones, the Sex Pistols and Bruce Springsteen.

Crystal Palace FC — an amateur club from 1861, and a professional side from 1905 — were ousted from their home in the shadow of Paxton’s building by the outbreak of the First World War, when the site was requisitioned by the British Navy.

Advertisement

They then played home matches at south London’s Herne Hill velodrome and then the Nest — a ground in the Selhurst area — before settling at Selhurst Park from 1924. But they have been tempted by a return to their spiritual home up the hill several times over the 102 years since. It has always felt like a possibility, even if it has never been realised.

Until the recent redevelopment of their academy site in nearby Beckenham, Palace’s youngest academy players were hosted in a dome up at the NSC, maintaining the long-standing link. Some of their reserve-team fixtures were played there at the turn of the millennium, too.

Yet the stadium’s most recent brush with football was as a home ground for Croydon FC, of Division One of the Southern Counties East League (step 10 of the English pyramid), who briefly relocated there in 2020, having been prevented from using Croydon Arena by the Covid-19 pandemic.

The NSC’s capacity was 16,000 at the time, but 213 supporters filtered in to watch Croydon’s first competitive match on December 5 — a 4-3 win over Athletic Newham.

There have been at least four occasions in the modern era when Crystal Palace have given serious consideration to a return up the hill.

The first was in 1989, overseen by the club’s then chairman Ron Noades.

In August that year, the Croydon Advertiser reported the club’s intentions, quoting Noades as saying: “Everyone talks about new stadia for the 21st century. Here, just up the (Sydenham) hill, is the opportunity. The athletics stands would have to come down and the arena re-created to suit football, but the site is ideal for a super stadium. There is so much space and parking for all.

“It’s the community thing that attracts me and the advantages are enormous at the Palace Centre.”

Advertisement

In October 1989, Noades told the Advertiser he was looking to build a 60,000 seater stadium for football and other sports, with a £10m ($13.4m) sale of Selhurst Park part-funding a £15m redevelopment scheme.

However, the Advertiser reported the length of the lease and level of control over the site as potential stumbling blocks.

Despite that, Palace made a formal approach just over a year later. The local Norwood Society reported in its quarterly review of February 1992 that Palace had made two applications for the construction of a new stadium in the park. Palace initially applied to build the new ground adjoining the existing NSC, while the second application was to rebuild the sports centre and ensure it accommodated both football and athletics.

Both proposals would have brought Palace a 35,000-seater stadium with 250 executive boxes and parking space for 2,500 cars. The Norwood Society, which has a sub-committee that reviews planning applications made in the local area, objected to these plans.

The application received in December 1991 ended up being rejected on 11 grounds.

Bromley Council determined that the scheme would be contrary to several policies of London’s unitary development plan, while the “site coverage, scale and bulk of the development” was considered to be “detrimental to the character of the park and its locality and detract from local views”.

Furthermore, it was considered “detrimental to the character and appearance of the Crystal Palace Park Conservation Area” and would fail to preserve or enhance the area, while also being counterproductive to the setting of listed buildings of architectural or historic interest.

The NSC was included in Bromley Council’s list of buildings of local architectural or historic interest which should be retained unless a replacement or adjacent project of exceptional architectural merit was proposed. The decision notice also noted that the existing roads around the park were inadequate to cope with the area’s traffic, and that major events held at the NSC and/or the park tended to exacerbate those problems.

Advertisement

Without an access and traffic impact analysis, it was considered that matches at the proposed stadium would “impose an unacceptable demand on the highway network to the detriment of the free flow of traffic and conditions of general safety in this and adjacent (London) boroughs”.

It also cited a need for “radical improvements to public transport servicing the area”, while adding that “crowds and heavy traffic associated with events at the stadium would be detrimental to the residential character and amenities of the area”.

The proposal was also said to be “detrimental to the continued public enjoyment of Crystal Palace Park’s recreational, sporting and other facilities, and its historic landscape”.

Palace, who finished third in the top division of English football in 1990-91, had been thwarted. They ended up redeveloping the Holmesdale end at Selhurst Park, replacing its terracing with a two-tier stand that opened in 1995.

In 2002, Palace, then owned by Simon Jordan, were tentatively sounded out in the hope that a football stadium would help supplement the return of international athletics competitions to the NSC site.

They were not alone, with fellow London sides Fulham, Wimbledon — who had yet to move to Milton Keynes — and Brentford among the other potential tenants. Yet nothing progressed.

A proposed multiplex cinema scheme had collapsed a year earlier, in May 2001, amid vehement opposition. The then mayor of London, Ken Livingstone, had expressed his opposition to it during a Mayor’s Question Time session in October 2000.

“I do, however, remain implacably opposed to the construction of a huge leisure centre on this sensitive site, served by a vast car park on its roof,” he said. “The probable uses — a multiplex cinema, fast-food restaurant, nightclubs and drinking venues — are not appropriate for Paxton’s historic Crystal Palace Park, and should be located in town centres.”

A decade later, in 2012, Palace considered the site again.

The club, in the second-tier Championship and now stewarded by Steve Parish and the CPFC 2010 consortium, started a consultation in July 2010 and, a year later, unveiled plans to build a new 40,000-seater stadium on the NSC site while also redeveloping the adjacent indoor sports complex, including its aquatic centre, and building a replacement athletics track.

Advertisement

That arena would initially have started life at a reduced 25,000-seat capacity, but would accommodate 50 executive boxes, a VIP suite, two banqueting lounges capable of housing 800 people, and extensive bar, shop and media facilities.

The initial phase was projected to cost around £50million, with money being raised from the sale of Selhurst Park.

There were positive noises from both Croydon and Bromley councils — which, alongside the districts of Lambeth, Southwark and Lewisham, converge around the site — with quotes from both council leaders. A second sports team playing in the stadium was to be explored, potentially from rugby union, and there was scope for a hotel and an elite sports academy.

The site’s leaseholder at the time was the London Development Agency (LDA), the regional development agency for Greater London, which was running at a significant deficit. Palace had spoken directly to the LDA, Greenwich Leisure — which ran the NSC — and the mayor’s office before making their proposals public.

“It is encouraging to see people coming forward with positive, innovative solutions for the future of Crystal Palace,” said Kate Hoey, who at the time was both the mayor’s commissioner for sport and a Member of Parliament.

“Crystal Palace FC has been at the heart of that community for well over 100 years, and I know they have been working hard to secure the support of all the key local stakeholders. I welcome their interest in the site and look forward to seeing more detail on what they have to offer to the local community and to London as a whole.”

At the time, the decision had yet to be made on what would happen to London’s 2012 Olympic Stadium in Stratford, east London, after the Games. Tottenham Hotspur wanted to develop the NSC as part of a deal that would see them move to the Olympic Stadium, but they were in competition with West Ham United.

Advertisement

Tottenham’s proposal was ultimately rejected in favour of that of West Ham, who would move from their traditional home of Upton Park. That, in turn, would theoretically leave Palace free to pursue their own stadium in Crystal Palace Park.

“The moment that, along with West Ham, we won the battle for the Olympic Stadium, the athletics stadium at Crystal Palace Park effectively became a white elephant,” Ed Warner who, at the time of the proposals, was chairman of UK Athletics, tells The Athletic.

“It was far too big for anything we would need in London, because the idea was that the Olympic Stadium would be it for athletics for the next 50 years. All you need in Crystal Palace is a club facility capable of area championships and domestic competition. That’s nothing like the scale of the stadium that’s there right now.

“As a result, that stadium is crumbling, which from an athletics perspective is very sad and needs to be sorted.”

Parish entered into the planning process but, after consultation with Bromley Council, was quickly told it was effectively an impossible build. Sources familiar with the proposals, granted anonymity to protect relationships, were under the impression the club would face a decade of discussions with the various councils, and would probably end up being thwarted by objections from locals.

A meeting was held with residents, and the club left those talks convinced a move would be a no-go. Like Noades, Parish eventually decided redeveloping Selhurst Park was simpler, with planning permission for a new main stand granted in principle in April 2018.

However, in 2020, Palace briefly revisited a return to the park.

With no progress being made on the redevelopment of Selhurst, the club — now established in the Premier League — had made representations to the relevant bodies about a potential move ‘home’ and drew up plans for what that might look like. A presentation was shown to Croydon Council in the process.

Advertisement

Any new stadium would have been largely tucked away close to the existing Crystal Palace railway station, with a club facility and indoor space for athletics which would have taken up a relatively small space.

But the prospect of Palace returning was never realistic.

The issues which had previously blocked a return merely flared up again.

That the improvement of transport links would have implications for five London boroughs — the park is in the borough of Bromley — makes securing political agreement across the board difficult. The local residents would whip up fierce opposition, too. Challenges would make the project time-consuming and expensive.

So, instead, the club pressed on with the Selhurst Park project and, in June, demolition began at the houses in neighbouring Wooderson Close, marking the final enabling works before the redevelopment begins in earnest.

Some will be dismayed that, when the NSC is eventually renovated, the football club once established there will not be at the forefront of the project. But there will be pride that athletics will be hosted in a spruced-up area.

It has been neglected for far too long.
